qs.q: An epidemiologist evaluates an outbreak of acute watery diarrhea in an institutionalized geriatric ward. Which demographic feature strongly points away from rotavirus as the primary causative agent in this adult setting?
qs.e: Rotavirus primarily causes severe gastroenteritis in infants and young children, making outbreaks in elderly adults atypical.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - November 13,

qs.q: A public health investigation reviews seasonal gastroenteritis outbreaks in daycare centers. An outbreak caused by calicivirus typically shows which epidemiological feature compared to rotavirus?
o: Higher frequency during warm summer months
Extended duration of fecal viral shedding
qs.e: Caliciviruses frequently affect older children and adults, whereas rotavirus predominantly targets infants.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - November 6,

qs.q: A 3-year-old child develops acute watery diarrhea while attending a daycare center. Laboratory analysis isolates a rotavirus strain. Which intrinsic biological property of this viral agent primarily accounts for its ability to cause extensive outbreaks in pediatric populations?
o: High environmental stability conferred by a robust double-layered protein capsid structure
Rapid systemic viremia leading to widespread secondary mucosal seeding events
Persistent latent infection established within deep submucosal lymphoid tissues
Continuous antigenic drift of outer envelope glycoproteins during replication
Direct inactivation of circulating host neutralizing antibodies via secreted enzymes
qs.e: Rotaviruses possess a sturdy double-layered capsid that resists environmental degradation and stomach acid.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - October 30,

qs.q: An epidemiological investigation of an outbreak involving three distinct pathogens—Vibrio cholerae, Entamoeba histolytica, and Rotavirus—reveals a commonality in how they spread through human populations. What is their shared characteristic?
qs.e: Vibrio cholerae, Entamoeba histolytica, and Rotavirus are all transmitted primarily via the fecal-oral route.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Microbiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which age group typically shows the highest incidence of Rotavirus and Nontyphoidal Salmonella (NTS) infections?
qs.e: The incidence of rotavirus and NTS are highest in infancy. Shigellosis peaks in 1-4 year olds, while other pathogens show different age distributions.

qs.q: How does the typical duration of diarrhea caused by enteric adenovirus compare to that caused by rotavirus?
qs.e: Enteric adenovirus infections tend to be more prolonged, lasting 7 to 10 days, whereas rotavirus recovery generally occurs within 7 days.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of rotavirus infection in children?
qs.e: Rotavirus symptoms usually begin with vomiting followed by frequent watery, nonbloody stools. The diarrhea lacks fecal leukocytes, and recovery generally occurs within 7 days.

ai.title: Rotavirus Gastroenteritis
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Rotavirus is the leading viral cause of acute diarrhoea in children under five, especially in low‑resource settings. Clinical focus is on recognising dehydration, ruling out bacterial mimics, and providing supportive care while avoiding unnecessary antibiotics.

sections.p: Rotavirus is a double‑stranded RNA virus of the Reoviridae family. It infects enterocytes, causing villous blunting and secretory diarrhoea. In East Africa, outbreaks are common in the dry season and among children who have not completed the full vaccine series.
b: Highly contagious; 10–1000 virions can cause infection
Vaccination reduces severity but does not eliminate infection

sections.p: The virus has a triple‑layered capsid and a segmented genome. It is resistant to drying and survives on surfaces for days. The VP4 and VP7 proteins are the main antigens targeted by vaccines.
Fecal‑oral route dominates; contaminated hands, food, water, and fomites spread the virus. The virus enters the small intestine, replicates in enterocytes, and is shed in stool for up to 10 days.
Acute gastroenteritis characterised by watery diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. Dehydration is the main threat. Severe cases may progress to hypovolaemic shock.
Clinical diagnosis is based on history of acute diarrhoea and vomiting in a child <5 years. Laboratory confirmation is optional but useful in outbreaks.

t.b: Positive confirms viral etiology; negative does not rule out if clinical picture fits
Same as ELISA but quicker; useful when ELISA unavailable
Rule out bacterial causes if fever >38.5°C or bloody stools

sections.p: Supportive care is the cornerstone. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) with zinc is first line. Antibiotics are not indicated unless bacterial infection is suspected. Vaccination and hygiene are preventive.

Remember that rotavirus diarrhoea is usually non‑bloody and resolves within 3–5 days. Dehydration severity guides fluid choice: oral for mild, IV for moderate‑severe. Avoid antibiotics unless dysentery or high fever persists.
Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Shigella, Campylobacter), amoebic dysentery, and cholera can mimic rotavirus but usually present with blood or high fever.
Stool microscopy may miss viral pathogens; a negative bacterial culture does not exclude rotavirus. Zinc levels may be normal despite deficiency.
Treat the underlying dehydration first. Monitor urine output, vital signs, and weight. If the child is unable to take ORS, give isotonic IV fluids. Reassure parents and educate on handwashing.
Rotavirus vaccine (monovalent or pentavalent) is given orally at 6, 10, and 14 weeks. In East Africa, coverage is variable; missed doses increase severity.
b: Avoid vaccine in children with severe malnutrition or cholera

sections.p: Severe dehydration can lead to shock, electrolyte imbalance, and death. Rarely, rotavirus can cause encephalopathy or myocarditis.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, lethargy, poor skin turgor, reduced urine output), persistent vomiting preventing ORS, blood in stool, high fever >38.5°C, or any sign of shock

faq.a: No, bloody stools usually indicate bacterial or amoebic infection.
Yes, zinc reduces duration and severity of diarrhoea in children under five.

faq.q: Do we give antibiotics for rotavirus?
faq.a: No, antibiotics are not indicated unless bacterial infection is suspected.

exam: A 12‑month‑old boy presents with 4 days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting. He is lethargic and has sunken eyes. What is the first step in management? — Assess dehydration severity, start ORS, give IV fluids if moderate‑severe.

A child with rotavirus diarrhoea develops a fever of 39°C. What is the most appropriate next step? — Re‑evaluate for bacterial superinfection; consider stool culture and start antibiotics only if dysentery or persistent fever.
A 2‑year‑old with rotavirus has a normal stool microscopy. What does this tell you? — Microscopy is not useful for viral detection; rely on clinical picture and antigen tests.
A child missed the third dose of rotavirus vaccine. What is the likely clinical consequence? — Increased risk of severe diarrhoea and higher mortality in outbreaks.
Why is zinc supplementation recommended in rotavirus diarrhoea? — Zinc shortens illness duration and reduces relapse rates.
What is the WHO dehydration grading for a child with 3–4 wet diapers per day? — Mild dehydration (1–5 wet diapers).
